title: Human Impact on the Environment
seo_title: Grade 11 Life Sciences: Human Impact on the Environment Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 11 Life Sciences: Human impact on the environment
standard_text: Human influences on the atmosphere (the greenhouse effect, climate change, ozone depletion); water availability and quality; food security; loss of biodiversity (habitat destruction, poaching, alien invasive species); solid waste; sustainable practices. (summary of CAPS Life Sciences, Grade 11, Life Sciences: Human impact on the environment)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Life Sciences worksheets (CAPS): climate change, water quality, food security, loss of biodiversity, alien species, solid waste and sustainability. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Burning fossil fuels adds CO₂, which enhances the greenhouse effect.
key_sub: Alien invasive plants use a lot of water and replace indigenous plants.
body_html:
How to think about it

Burning coal and petrol releases carbon dioxide, which traps more heat and causes global warming and climate change. CFCs damage the ozone layer, which protects us from UV radiation. Water is polluted by sewage, fertilisers, industry and acid mine drainage.

Biodiversity is lost through habitat destruction, poaching (for example rhino horn), over-exploitation and alien invasive species such as wattle and water hyacinth. Food security needs sustainable farming. Reducing, reusing and recycling waste, and conserving water and energy help protect the environment.

Example

Why are alien plants such as Port Jackson willow removed?

Water and indigenous plants

Answer: they use lots of water and outcompete indigenous plants

Example

Which gas mainly causes the enhanced greenhouse effect?

From burning fuels

Answer: carbon dioxide

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the greenhouse effect itself is bad (without it Earth would be too cold).
  • Mixing up the ozone hole and global warming.
  • Thinking recycling is the only way to reduce waste.

faq.q: What is the Working for Water programme?
faq.a: A South African programme that clears alien invasive plants to save water and create jobs.

faq.q: How does climate change affect food security?
faq.a: Droughts, floods and higher temperatures reduce crop yields.

items.q: Jabu reads: “Hunters remove most of the sea otters from a coast.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish

items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Yusuf learns: Sea otters were overhunted. What happened to the sea urchins?
c: They increased and ate the kelp forests.

items.q: Precious wants to know whether a new bus line reduces air pollution. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: check once on a single day

measure air quality and traffic for several months before and after
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: How can fertiliser runoff harm a lake?
c: It causes algae to grow quickly, and when the algae die, oxygen levels drop.

items.q: What could happen to apple harvests if bee numbers fall a lot?
c: Fewer flowers are pollinated, so fewer apples grow.

items.q: Why do some flowers have bright petals and a sweet scent?

items.q: What does the Indigenous idea of 'Seven Generations' teach?

items.q: Which is a benefit of buying local food?

items.q: Which action helps pollinators?

items.q: Which is an example of habitat restoration?

items.q: Ravi's class studies this problem: “Forest animals are trapped in small patches between farms.” Which solution would best protect biodiversity?
c: connect the patches with wildlife corridors
items.e: It solves the cause of the problem while protecting species.

items.q: Which technology is designed to reduce this impact: farms wasting water through flood irrigation?
c: wildlife crossings over or under roads
items.e: Engineers design solutions that reduce harm to natural systems.

items.q: Musa's class studies this problem: “A wetland was drained and nearby towns now flood.” Which solution would best protect biodiversity?
items.e: It solves the cause of the problem while protecting species.

items.q: What is crop rotation?
c: growing the same crop every year
growing different crops in a field in different years
items.e: Rotation keeps soil healthy, breaks pest cycles and can add nitrogen (with legumes such as beans).

items.q: Ethan's class studies this problem: “Bee populations are falling near farms.” Which solution would best protect biodiversity?
c: plant wildflower strips and reduce pesticide use
items.e: It solves the cause of the problem while protecting species.

items.q: Which technology is designed to reduce this impact: soil washing off steep farm fields?
items.e: Engineers design solutions that reduce harm to natural systems.

items.q: Why does using less fertiliser protect lakes?
c: fertiliser adds too much salt to the ocean
extra nitrogen and phosphorus wash into water and cause algal blooms
items.e: When the algae die, decomposers use up the oxygen, and fish can die.

items.q: Which is an example of adapting to climate change rather than slowing it?
c: switching from coal to wind power
building higher flood walls and planting trees for shade in cities
items.e: Mitigation reduces the cause; adaptation reduces the damage.

items.q: Ethan's class studies this problem: “An invasive vine is smothering native plants.” Which solution would best protect biodiversity?
c: remove the vine and replant native species
items.e: It solves the cause of the problem while protecting species.

items.q: How do wetlands help reduce the effects of climate change?
c: they store carbon and soak up floodwater
items.e: Peatlands and marshes hold large amounts of carbon in waterlogged soil.

items.q: Which change reduces greenhouse gas emissions from transportation?
c: taking transit, cycling or using electric vehicles charged from clean electricity
idling the car to keep it warm
items.e: Most transport emissions come from burning petrol and diesel.

items.q: Which action improves soil health on a farm?
c: adding compost and keeping plants growing on the soil
packing the soil with heavy machines
items.e: Organic matter feeds soil organisms and helps the soil hold water.

items.q: What is the Three Sisters planting method?
c: watering crops three times a day
planting three rows of the same crop
growing corn, beans and squash together so each plant helps the others
items.e: Corn supports the beans, beans add nitrogen and squash leaves shade the soil and keep moisture in.

items.q: Which technology is designed to reduce this impact: dams blocking salmon from swimming upstream?
c: wildlife crossings over or under roads
items.e: Engineers design solutions that reduce harm to natural systems.

items.q: What is a carbon sink?
c: something that takes in more carbon dioxide than it releases, such as a forest or the ocean
items.e: Oceans, soils and forests remove CO₂ from the atmosphere.

items.q: Why does cutting down a forest add to climate change?
c: trees produce carbon dioxide in photosynthesis
fewer trees take in CO₂, and burning or rotting wood releases stored carbon
forests block greenhouse gases from reaching space
items.e: Forests are carbon sinks; removing them turns a sink into a source.

items.q: Which technology is designed to reduce this impact: fertiliser runoff causing dead zones?
c: cover crops and buffer strips of plants
items.e: Engineers design solutions that reduce harm to natural systems.

items.q: What is a climate change indicator?
c: a measurement that shows how the climate is changing, such as sea-ice extent or average temperature
items.e: Indicators are tracked over many years to show trends.

items.q: Which human impact are wildlife crossings over or under roads designed to reduce?
c: car exhaust releasing carbon monoxide and smog gases
highways cutting animals off from their habitat
items.e: Match the solution to the problem.
